create.name: Shao Shan Temple
create.bio:
Shao Shan Temple is a small Soto Zen temple in the woods of Woodbury, in northern Vermont, registered with the Soto school of Japan. Rev. Taihaku Priest, who trained at Hokyoji monastery in Fukui and received transmission from Tanaka Shinkai Roshi, built it from 1997 and opened it in 2000; she served as its abbot and for some years as president of the Soto Zen Buddhist Association, and died in 2021. Her dharma heir Rev. Kenzan Seidenberg, ordained by her in 2008 and recognised by the Soto school as an international teacher, is now abbot in residence.

The temple keeps a weekly rhythm of early-morning zazen with a short service, some sittings joined online, a Wednesday dharma discussion, Friday evening sitting and a Saturday programme with a talk. Through the year there are one-day zazenkai, weekend sesshin and the week-long Rohatsu sesshin in December, a precepts ceremony, seasonal ceremonies at the solstices and equinoxes, a monthly family programme and a summer camp. Newcomers begin with an introductory morning, and all public programmes are offered without a fee, supported by donations.

courses.title: Rohatsu Sesshin
courses.description: The temple's week of intensive sitting and walking meditation in early December, marking the Buddha's enlightenment. Like the other retreats it is meant for people who already practise at the temple regularly.

courses.title: Introduction to Shao Shan Temple
courses.description: An hour-long first visit for everyone new to the temple: an outline of its programmes, meditation instruction, a short tour and time for questions. Advance registration through the contact form is appreciated.

courses.title: Study Group
courses.description: Zazen followed by discussion of a chosen Buddhist text or theme, drawing on many traditions, held online. Weekly attendance is not required, and newcomers attend an introduction first.

free_resources.title: Chants
free_resources.description: Texts and audio recordings of the chants used at the temple, among them the dedication verse, the robe verse, the Kannon chant and the three refuges, for learning at home.
